title: Dedicated Burst Capacity — Unit Economics Sensitivity (v1)
content:
Redwood Inference — Finance (FP&A)
Doc: Dedicated Burst Capacity — Unit Economics Sensitivity (v1)
Owner: Rishi Malhotra
Last updated: 2025-02-21

Purpose
- Quick sensitivity model to understand gross margin impact of offering “burst capacity” to Dedicated customers.
- Focus is *incremental* economics of burst pools (shared, Redwood-managed) under different utilization + pricing assumptions.
- Intended audience: Finance sponsor (Laura), Product (Lauren), Fleet (Vanessa/Keiko). Not customer-facing.

Summary (current read)
- Burst can be margin-accretive if (a) we price above effective all-in GPU cost, (b) we keep burst pool utilization in a healthy band (not too low, not saturating), and (c) we protect non-burst SLOs to avoid cost blowups and credits.
- Biggest economic risk is *low utilization* of burst pools (carrying cost) combined with aggressive customer pricing expectations.
- Second-order risk: retries/telemetry lag leading to double-counted usage or “free” load (ENG-4827 + billing idempotency work is gating).

Key definitions
- Baseline Dedicated: customer’s committed reserved capacity (e.g., 16x H100). This has its own contract economics; not modeled here.
- Burst: temporary incremental capacity above baseline, served out of a regional/hardware burst pool.
- Unit of measure (assumption for modeling): burst GPU-hours (metered via GPU-seconds aggregated per tenant, then converted).
  - Note: engineering may meter tokens + GPU seconds; this model treats the billable unit as GPU-hours for simplicity.

Model scope / what is included in “cost”
Included in burst cost per GPU-hour:
- GPU infra cost (amortized) or cloud GPU spend equivalent
- Hosting overhead allocation (power, rack, networking where applicable)
- Fleet management overhead (spares, burn-in, maintenance) as % uplift
- SRE/ops overhead allocation (lightweight % uplift)

Not included (tracked separately or too uncertain in v1):
- Cost of capital / procurement financing differences by region
- Potential SLA credits due to neighbor impact incidents (should be mitigated by guardrails; see notes)
- Sales discounting variability (captured as price haircut in sensitivity)

Inputs (editable assumptions)
These are “model knobs” used to generate the sensitivity tables.

Table A — Cost assumptions (per GPU-hour, all-in)
Hardware class | Region    | All-in cost/hr (C) | Notes
H100          | us-east   | $2.35              | blended (owned + colo ops + overhead)
H100          | eu-west   | $2.65              | higher power + lower scale
L40S          | us-east   | $0.78              | lower capex + higher availability
L40S          | eu-west   | $0.90              | +15% vs us-east

Notes on cost inputs
- These are placeholders derived from internal capacity planning ranges; fleet will update once procurement quotes + effective utilization baseline are locked.
- Overhead factor currently baked into C (includes ~18% ops uplift). If we switch to explicit overhead, keep consistent across scenarios.

Table B — Pool sizing + utilization assumptions
Parameter                              | Symbol | Default | Range tested
Burst pool size (GPUs)                 | N      | 256     | 64 / 128 / 256 / 512
Target average utilization of pool     | U      | 35%     | 15% / 25% / 35% / 50% / 70%
Billable fraction of utilized time     | Bf     | 92%     | 85%–98%
  (accounts for guardrail denials,
   internal load tests, maintenance)

Interpretation
- U is the most important driver. At low U, fixed pool carrying cost dominates.
- Bf captures non-billable consumption and leakage (e.g., warm spares, debug traffic, measurement error). Billing + idempotency should push Bf up.

Table C — Pricing assumptions (per GPU-hour)
Hardware class | Tier   | List price/hr (P) | Discount factor (D) | Effective price (Peff)
H100          | Gold   | $3.75              | 0.90                | $3.38
H100          | Silver | $3.25              | 0.90                | $2.93
L40S          | Gold   | $1.40              | 0.90                | $1.26
L40S          | Silver | $1.15              | 0.90                | $1.04

Notes
- D=0.90 approximates blended discounting for Dedicated enterprise deals (varies widely). Sensitivity below also tests D=0.80.
- We should align any tiering with admission priority semantics (gold/silver) so pricing matches actual QoS.

Core formulas (per pool, per month)
Assume 30-day month.
- Total available GPU-hours: H_total = N * 24 * 30
- Utilized GPU-hours: H_util = H_total * U
- Billable GPU-hours: H_bill = H_util * Bf

Revenue = H_bill * Peff
Cost    = H_total * C   (pool carrying cost)
Gross profit = Revenue - Cost
Gross margin % = (Revenue - Cost) / Revenue

Important: This treats the burst pool as a “capacity product” with an always-on cost base. If we can elastically scale pools with low lag and low risk, the effective cost base becomes closer to H_util, improving economics at low U.

Sensitivity results

1) H100 us-east (C=$2.35/hr). N=256 GPUs. Bf=92%. D=0.90.

Table 1 — Gross margin by utilization (Gold vs Silver)
Utilization U | Gold Peff=$3.38 | Silver Peff=$2.93
15%           | -145%           | -196%
25%           | -47%            | -76%
35%           | 4%              | -13%
50%           | 31%             | 21%
70%           | 47%             | 41%

Interpretation
- Break-even for Gold is ~33–35% utilization with current assumptions.
- Silver tier is not viable unless utilization is consistently >~40% or costs drop.
- This is *pool-level* margin; product-level margin depends on how much dedicated baseline margin we attribute elsewhere.

2) H100 eu-west (C=$2.65/hr). N=128 GPUs (smaller initial pool). Bf=92%. D=0.90.

Table 2 — Gross margin by utilization (Gold only)
Utilization U | Gold Peff=$3.38
15%           | -185%
25%           | -76%
35%           | -17%
50%           | 14%
70%           | 34%

Interpretation
- eu-west is materially harder due to higher cost/hr.
- Recommendation: smaller initial eu-west pool + stricter enablement and/or higher eu-west burst price multiplier.

3) L40S us-east (C=$0.78/hr). N=256 GPUs. Bf=92%. D=0.90.

Table 3 — Gross margin by utilization
Utilization U | Gold Peff=$1.26 | Silver Peff=$1.04
15%           | -76%            | -112%
25%           | -13%            | -35%
35%           | 23%             | 10%
50%           | 45%             | 37%
70%           | 60%             | 55%

Interpretation
- L40S economics are more forgiving. Still, low utilization hurts.

4) Discounting risk (H100 us-east Gold). N=256, U=35%, Bf=92%.

Table 4 — Gross margin sensitivity to discount factor
Discount factor D | Effective price Peff | GM%
1.00              | $3.75                | 16%
0.90              | $3.38                | 4%
0.85              | $3.19                | -2%
0.80              | $3.00                | -9%

Interpretation
- If sales pushes >20% discounts on burst, pool economics go negative at 35% utilization.
- Finance ask: either enforce discount floors for burst line items, or require higher minimum commitment / pre-purchase of burst credits.

5) Billing leakage / non-billable fraction risk (H100 us-east Gold). N=256, U=35%, D=0.90.

Table 5 — GM% by billable fraction (Bf)
Bf     | GM%
85%    | -5%
90%    | 1%
92%    | 4%
95%    | 7%
98%    | 11%

Interpretation
- Metering quality matters. 5–10 pts of leakage changes margin meaningfully.
- Reinforces need for:
  - idempotency keys (avoid double-counting OR under-counting on retries)
  - clear admission outcomes (avoid “zombie” queueing that consumes capacity unbilled)
  - reconciliation jobs (Nadia/Cole workstream)

Scenario planning (what does this mean for GA packaging?)

Scenario S1 — Conservative launch (recommended for GA)
- Regions/hardware: start H100 us-east + L40S us-east; keep eu-west limited/allow-listed.
- Pricing: H100 Gold only at ~$3.75 list; allow mild discounting (<=10%) when paired with baseline commit.
- Controls: hard global fleet safety cap + per-tenant burst cap to prevent saturation and neighbor incidents.
- Expected economics: positive GM if pool U sustains ~35%+.

Scenario S2 — “Competitive pricing” (risk)
- Introduce Silver tier pricing broadly (H100 at ~$3.25 list, heavy discounting).
- Outcome: requires high utilization to avoid negative margin; also likely increases demand + saturation risk.

Scenario S3 — Regional multiplier
- Apply eu-west price uplift (e.g., +10–15% on burst) or smaller pools + higher scarcity pricing.
- Outcome: improves eu-west viability without forcing global price changes.

Operational/guardrail assumptions that impact economics (non-finance but real)
- If burst admission is too permissive and causes tail latency regressions, we may incur:
  - SLA credits
  - churn risk (hard to model but real)
  - engineering + SRE cost from incident response
- Guardrails that deny burst reduce revenue but protect baseline customers. We should treat that as an intentional product constraint and price burst as a premium feature.

Open questions / next steps
1) Metering unit: confirm billing will be GPU-seconds vs tokens vs “burst capacity units.” Align model once final.
2) Pool elasticity: can we autoscale burst pools with acceptable lag? If yes, update model to shift some cost from fixed to variable.
3) Tier-to-QoS mapping: if Gold/Silver tiers correspond to admission priority, model should include expected denial rates per tier (Bf differs by tier).
4) Regional costs: Fleet to provide updated C ranges (P10/P50/P90) by hardware class and region.
5) Discount policy: decide whether burst is non-discountable, discount-capped, or requires separate approval.

Decision support (Finance recommendation as of 2025-02-21)
- For H100 burst: keep a single premium tier at launch; avoid low-priced Silver for H100 until utilization is proven and/or costs reduce.
- Use regional multipliers or region-specific list pricing (especially eu-west) rather than absorbing cost deltas.
- Bake a minimum effective price floor into approvals (e.g., D >= 0.90 for burst line item unless Laura approves).
- Treat metering integrity as a GA gate (Bf >= ~92% equivalent); otherwise the product looks profitable but isn’t.

Appendix — Example calculations (H100 us-east, N=256, U=35%, Bf=92%)
- H_total = 256 * 24 * 30 = 184,320 GPU-hrs/month
- H_util  = 184,320 * 0.35 = 64,512 GPU-hrs
- H_bill  = 64,512 * 0.92 = 59,351 GPU-hrs
- Revenue (Gold Peff $3.38) = 59,351 * 3.38 = ~$200.6k
- Cost (C $2.35) = 184,320 * 2.35 = ~$433.1k
- Gross profit = -$232.5k (NOTE: This indicates an inconsistency if we treat the pool as fully fixed cost and only bill for utilized time; see below)

Important correction note (why the above looks wrong)
- The above reveals a modeling choice mismatch:
  - If burst pools are *fully dedicated/always-on capacity* with cost incurred for every GPU-hour regardless of utilization, then we must ensure U reflects the portion of the pool that is *actually provisioned/kept powered and reserved for bursting* vs “logical pool size.”
  - In current fleet thinking, “pool size” N is a *logical maximum*, but physical capacity may be opportunistic (borrowed from managed fleet, powered on as needed, or shared with internal workloads).
- Therefore in v1 tables above, interpret Cost as: Cost = (H_util / U_eff) * C where U_eff is effective utilization of the physically provisioned portion.

Action item
- Vanessa/Keiko to confirm whether burst pool capacity is:
  (A) hard-reserved GPUs (fixed cost), or
  (B) elastic/shared capacity with an SLO-protected admission cap (more variable cost).
- Once confirmed, we will publish v2 with consistent fixed vs variable cost treatment.

(End)
